newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Sihanouk, the cornerstone of modern Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Sihanouk, the cornerstone of modern Cambodia.

text.p: King Norodom Sihanouk, Cambodia's quixotic and colourful ruler who turned 74 on Thursday, has personified the country's tragic misfortunes through five decades of war and peace.
He has seen the end of a long and bitter civil war, the country's first free and fair election and the establishment of a reconciliation government and restoration of the monarchy.

Sihanouk has played a pivotal role in winning these gains as the only figure able to command the respect of the world community and the four rival factions, including the radical Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, that agreed to peace in 1991 after 21 years of strife.

More recently the king, setting the interests of the nation above personal distaste, agreed to a government request earlier this year by signing a royal pardon to Ieng Sary for his role in the genocide of more than one million people as foreign minister of the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.
Sihanouk's gesture has allowed peace talks to resume between the government and dissident Khmer Rouge leader.
His role as the promoter of peace and democracy and champion of human rights has removed some of the tarnish left by his autocratic rule of the 1950s and 1960s.

But recently Sihanouk has become no more than a cipher, a king who reigns but does not rule, and who is powerless to prevent a perceived drift towards autocracy and the eclipse of the royalists by his ersthwile socialist foes.

Sihanouk, the master manipulator and tactician, was ultimately outmanoeuvred by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, and acknowledged this in April 1996, telling Le Monde that the premier was Cambodia's real strongman.

Ironically Sihanouk has come full circle since his first entry on to the political stage, when he was unexpectedly chosen by the French colonial government to succeed his uncle, Sisowath Monivong, to the throne in September 1941.
The king's skills were not evident when the French engineered his accession in the belief that he would be more pliable than his uncle or the direct heir.
But Sihanouk was to take on the French and lead the ultimately successful independence crusade, which saw the French protectorate end in late 1953.

The first 10 years in the life of modern Cambodia are now seen by many as a golden age, but also a time when Sihanouk was able to impose an iron rule over political foes. His master stroke of abdicating in 1955 enabled him to pursue political ambitions unfettered by royal constraints.
The honeymoon began to sour in the 1960s as Sihanouk came down heavily on opponents while desperately trying to keep his country out of the growing conflagration in neighbouring Vietnam.
He courted West and East but annoyed conservatives and corrupt elements in business circles by rejecting U.S. aid in 1963 and cutting ties with Washington in 1965.

His balancing act almost kept Cambodia out of the war, although Sihanouk allowed China to ship arms to the communist Vietnamese through Cambodia. But at the same time left-wing opposition at home was growing and erupted into fighting after a peasant revolt in 1967.

In 1969 then-U.S. President Richard Nixon ordered the bombing of North Vietnam's Cambodian sanctuaries in a secret escalation of the conflict. During a trip to Moscow in 1970 Sihanouk was ousted in a U.S.-backed coup led by right-wing General Lon Nol.
He returned to the jungle to join communist fighters he had once contemptuously dubbed "Les Khmers Rouges", an alliance for which the flamboyant prince would pay heavily in future.

Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge used Sihanouk as a figurehead in the civil war which ended with their takeover in April 1975. They then held him prisoner in his palace while they conducted a systematic reign of terror lasting almost four years.

Though he had vowed never to become king again, Sihanouk was chosen head of state after a 1991 peace treaty officially ended the conflict, and in September 1993 he reclaimed the crown as a symbol of reconciliation and unity.
